title: How System Design Interviews Work
tagline: What this round actually tests, why it exists, and how to read the room.
summary: What the round tests and how it's graded — read this first.

sections.title: What a system design interview actually is

paragraphs: A system design interview is an open-ended, 35–60 minute conversation where the interviewer hands you a deliberately vague prompt — *"Design Twitter"*, *"Design a URL shortener"* — and asks you to architect a real, large-scale system on a whiteboard or shared doc. There is no single correct answer and no code to compile. You are being evaluated on how you **think**, **communicate**, and **make trade-offs** under ambiguity.

This is the complete opposite of a coding interview. In a coding round there is a hidden test suite and a right answer. Here, the interviewer is the test suite, and they care less about the final diagram than about the *reasoning* that produced it. Two candidates can draw nearly identical architectures and get opposite scores purely based on how they justified each decision.

The skill being measured is the everyday job of a senior engineer: take a fuzzy business need, turn it into concrete requirements, propose an architecture, and defend it against scale, failure, and cost. Companies use this round because it predicts on-the-job performance far better than puzzle-solving.

blocks.text: Think of it like an architect pitching a building. The client says "I want an office." A weak architect immediately sketches walls. A strong one asks: how many people? what budget? will it grow? earthquake zone? *Then* they draw — and they explain every choice. The drawing is the easy part; the questions and trade-offs are the job.

paragraphs: Behind the friendly chat, the interviewer is scoring you on a rubric. Almost every company's rubric reduces to the same five signals.

items.detail: Do you clarify before designing? Can you separate what the system *must* do (functional) from how *well* it must do it (non-functional)? Do you pick a sensible scope for the time available?
Do you follow a logical flow (requirements → estimation → API → data → high-level design → deep dive → bottlenecks) or do you jump around and forget pieces?
Do you know the building blocks (caches, queues, load balancers, databases) and can you go *deep* on at least one when pushed?
Every choice has a cost. Strong candidates say *"I'll use X because Y, accepting the downside Z."* This is the single highest-signal behaviour in the room.
Can the interviewer follow your thinking? Do you drive the conversation, manage time, and respond well to pushback?

blocks.title: The number one reason candidates fail
blocks.text: Not lack of knowledge — it's jumping straight to drawing boxes without clarifying requirements or estimating scale. The interviewer deliberately gives you an incomplete prompt to see if you'll ask. Silence and guessing read as inexperience.

sections.title: Junior vs senior: what bar you're held to

paragraphs: The *same question* is graded differently by level. Knowing your target bar tells you where to spend your study time. You are never penalised for exceeding the bar — but you must clear it.

rows: Solid fundamentals; can build a correct, simple design with guidance
Drives the whole problem independently; anticipates issues before being asked
Asks a few clarifying questions when prompted
Frames scope, calls out what's out-of-scope, states explicit assumptions
Knows what a load balancer, cache, and DB are and where they go
Knows *which* cache/DB and why, plus their failure modes and limits
Can compare two options when asked
Volunteers trade-offs constantly; reasons about cost, consistency, ops burden
Designs for 10x growth, partial failure, hot keys, and data loss
Goes deep on a bottleneck (e.g., the feed fan-out) with real numbers
blocks.caption: You don't need to be 'senior' to pass a senior loop on every axis — but consistently clearing the junior bar and showing senior instincts on a couple of axes is what gets offers.

blocks.title: If you're targeting new-grad / SDE-1
blocks.text: Master the **Fundamentals** and **Building Blocks** sections cold, learn the **framework**, and be able to walk through 4–5 **case studies** cleanly. That clears the bar. Don't over-index on exotic distributed-systems theory yet.

blocks.title: If you're targeting senior / staff
blocks.text: Everything above, *plus* the **Distributed Systems** section (consensus, replication, partitioning, idempotency), real capacity numbers, and the ability to deep-dive any single component for 10 minutes while reasoning about cost and operations.

paragraphs: This module is a sequenced curriculum, not a reference dump. The sections build on each other — read them in order the first time through, then use them as a reference later. Every lesson ends with an **interview cheat sheet** (the lines to memorise) and **practice questions** (because theory without practice is wasted).

items.title: Start Here
items.detail: This section. Get the mindset and the roadmap so nothing feels random.

items.title: Fundamentals
items.detail: The vocabulary — scalability, availability, consistency, CAP, latency numbers. You can't discuss trade-offs without these words.

items.title: Building Blocks
items.detail: The components you'll place on every diagram: load balancers, caches, CDNs, databases, queues, gateways.

items.title: Distributed Systems
items.detail: The hard parts: replication, sharding, consensus, consistent hashing, idempotency. This is the senior differentiator.

items.title: Case Studies
items.detail: Full, structured walkthroughs of the classic questions. This is where everything clicks together.

items.title: Interview Playbook
items.detail: The repeatable framework, estimation cheats, and communication tactics. Read before any real interview.

blocks.title: Language doesn't matter here
blocks.text: System design is language-agnostic — you reason about boxes, data, and arrows, not syntax. Where this module shows code (data models, API shapes, a rate-limiter, an ID generator), snippets are short and the idea transfers directly to C++, Python, or Java.

cheatsheet: The interview grades reasoning and communication, not a 'correct' diagram.
Five signals: requirements/scoping, structured approach, breadth+depth, trade-offs, communication.
The #1 failure is drawing before clarifying — always gather requirements first.
Every decision should be stated as 'I choose X because Y, accepting trade-off Z.'
Junior bar = correct simple design + fundamentals; senior bar = drive it, go deep, design for 10x and failure.

questions.prompt: Your interviewer says only "Design Instagram." What is the *first* thing you do, and why?
questions.hint: What separates a strong candidate from a weak one in the first two minutes?
answer: Do **not** start drawing. Begin by clarifying requirements to scope the problem. Ask functional questions (do we need photo upload, feed, follows, likes, comments, stories, search?) and non-functional questions (how many daily active users, read-vs-write ratio, latency expectations, consistency needs?).

Then explicitly state scope and assumptions: e.g., *"I'll focus on photo upload, generating a home feed, and the follow graph; I'll treat stories, DMs, and ads as out of scope for time."* This shows the interviewer you can turn ambiguity into a concrete, bounded problem — the core senior signal.
keyPoints: Resist the urge to draw immediately
State scope and assumptions out loud
Confirm scale (DAU, read/write ratio) before estimating
followUps: How would your design change if it were 1 million vs 1 billion users?
Which of those features is hardest at scale and why?

questions.prompt: You finish a clean design and the interviewer asks, "Why did you choose a NoSQL database here instead of SQL?" You didn't really think about it. How do you recover?
questions.hint: Honesty plus a trade-off beats a confident wrong answer.
answer: Don't bluff. Reason out loud about the actual trade-off for *this* workload: if the access pattern is simple key lookups with massive write volume and you can tolerate eventual consistency, a NoSQL store scales horizontally more easily. If you need multi-row transactions, joins, or strong consistency, SQL is a better fit.

Then convert it into a decision: *"Given our write-heavy, key-based access and relaxed consistency, I'll keep NoSQL — but if we needed transactional guarantees for, say, payments, I'd switch that part to a relational store."* Showing you can re-derive the choice from requirements is exactly what they want.
keyPoints: Never bluff a confident wrong answer
Re-derive the choice from the workload's access pattern and consistency needs
End with a concrete decision and the condition that would change it
followUps: When would you use both SQL and NoSQL in the same system?
